kits.familyName: Getting ready to meet a client
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. In fifteen minutes you are meeting a {client} for the first time.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you have a first meeting with a new {client} at 10 a.m.
pressure: {coworker3} says {client.plural} do not care about the small stuff.
detail: The meeting will be in the front office.
{Lead|the} will join for the last few minutes.

tiers.1: Letting someone know you will be late comes before anything else.
tiers.2: Meeting the dress code shows respect for the {client} and the workplace.
tiers.3: Preparation shows the {client} you take their time seriously.
tiers.4: Your full attention belongs to the {client} during the meeting.
tiers.5: Small courtesies matter once the basics are covered.

fact: You are running about ten minutes behind for the meeting.
clear: You already messaged the {client} that you would be ten minutes late.
issues.done: the {client} already knows you will be late
issues.action: Let the {client} know now that you are running ten minutes late.
issues.brief: tell the {client} you will be late
issues.reason: A quick heads-up respects the {client}'s time and keeps the first impression positive.
issues.lesson: If you will be late, let people know before the start time.

shortcut.text: Arrive when you can and apologize at the start.
shortcut.why: An apology after the fact does not give the {client} the chance to plan.
shortcut.mis: Apologizing later is as good as warning ahead.

fact: The workplace dress code calls for closed-toe shoes, and you are wearing sandals.
issues.action: Change into the closed-toe shoes the dress code calls for.
issues.reason: Following the dress code shows respect and represents the workplace well.
issues.lesson: Follow your workplace's dress code, especially when meeting others.

shortcut.text: Keep the sandals, since the {client} will not look at your feet.
shortcut.why: The dress code applies whether or not anyone notices.
shortcut.mis: Rules only matter if someone notices.

clear: You changed into closed-toe shoes before leaving home.
issues.done: you are already wearing closed-toe shoes

fact: You have not looked at the {client}'s request since it arrived last week.
clear: You reviewed the {client}'s request and made notes this morning.
issues.action: Spend a few minutes reviewing the {client}'s request before the meeting.
issues.reason: Knowing the request shows the {client} you are prepared and respect their time.
issues.lesson: Prepare before meetings so you can represent the workplace well.

shortcut.text: Ask the {client} to explain the request again from the start.
shortcut.why: Asking a {client} to repeat what they already sent suggests you did not prepare.

fact: Your phone keeps buzzing with personal texts.
issues.action: Silence your phone and put it away for the meeting.
issues.brief: silence and put away your phone
issues.reason: Checking a phone in a meeting signals the {client} is not your priority.
issues.lesson: Give people your full attention by putting your phone away.

shortcut.text: Keep the phone on the table so you can glance at urgent texts.
shortcut.brief: keep the phone on the table
shortcut.why: Glancing at texts during a meeting is distracting and disrespectful.
shortcut.mis: Quick glances at a phone go unnoticed.

fact: You have forgotten the {client}'s name, though it is on the meeting invite.
issues.action: Check the meeting invite for the name before you go in.
issues.brief: check the invite for the name
issues.reason: Using someone's name correctly is a basic courtesy that makes a good impression.
issues.lesson: Small courtesies, like using names correctly, build professional relationships.

shortcut.text: Avoid using the {client}'s name during the meeting.
shortcut.why: Avoiding the name can feel cold when the invite has it.
shortcut.mis: Avoiding a name is as good as remembering it.

proceed.text: Greet the {client} warmly and start the meeting on time.
proceed.why: You are prepared, dressed appropriately and on time, so the meeting can start.
proceed.lesson: Preparation and punctuality let you make a strong professional impression.

generic.text: Ask {coworker} to take the meeting so you can relax.
generic.why: The meeting is yours. Handing it off without reason is unprofessional.
generic.mis: Avoiding pressure is a good reason to hand off work.

generic.text: Start the meeting with a joke about how hectic your morning was.
generic.why: Opening with your own stress makes the meeting about you instead of the {client}.
generic.mis: Complaining about your day builds rapport.

overcaution.text: Ask {lead|the} to run the whole meeting instead of you.
overcaution.why: You are ready. Handing the meeting over is unnecessary.
overcaution.mis: Supervisors should run every client meeting.

setup: You have a first meeting with a new {client} at {workplace|the} this morning.

prep: You have not looked at the {client}'s request yet.
dress: Your shoes do not meet the dress code.

steps.text: Review the request and make notes
Arrive at the meeting room a few minutes early
Greet the {client} and start the meeting

rel: Preparation comes before you go to the meeting.
You need to be there before you greet the {client}.
Silence your phone before the meeting starts.
Your notes are for the meeting.
process.lesson: Prepare, meet the dress code, arrive early, silence distractions, then begin.

review.notes: Dress code stated as workplace policy.

setup: You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}, in the middle of a normal workday.

fact: You are about to reply-all to a message sent to the whole company with a personal joke.
issues.action: Reply only to the person you meant, or skip the reply.
issues.reason: A reply-all joke fills everyone's inbox and may not land well with people who do not know you.
issues.lesson: Think about who will read a message before you send it.

shortcut.text: Send it to everyone, since a joke will lighten the day.
shortcut.why: Hundreds of people did not ask for the joke, and some may find it unprofessional.

fact: You need to take a long personal call, and coworkers are working right next to you.
issues.short: the personal call in a shared area
issues.action: Step somewhere private to take the call.
issues.reason: A long personal call in a shared space distracts coworkers.
issues.lesson: Respect shared spaces by keeping personal calls private.

shortcut.text: Take the call on speaker so you can keep working.
shortcut.why: Speakerphone in a shared area disturbs everyone nearby.
shortcut.mis: Multitasking on a call is efficient.

fact: After a frustrating day, you start writing a public post complaining about a {client} by name.
issues.action: Delete the post and talk the frustration over privately instead.
issues.reason: A public complaint about a named {client} reflects on you and your workplace, and it can hurt the {client}.
issues.lesson: What you post publicly represents you and your workplace.

shortcut.text: Post it, since it is your own account.
shortcut.why: Your own account is still public, and naming a {client} can harm them and your workplace.
shortcut.mis: Personal accounts have nothing to do with work.

fact: You need a stapler, and the only one is on {coworker}'s desk while {coworker} is away.
issues.action: Borrow it, then return it right away with a quick note saying thanks.
issues.reason: A short, open borrow with a note is courteous; keeping it or hiding the borrow is not.
issues.lesson: Treat coworkers' things with courtesy: ask or tell, and return them quickly.

shortcut.text: Take it to your desk and keep it for the week.
shortcut.why: Keeping a coworker's things without asking is inconsiderate.
shortcut.mis: Shared items belong to whoever needs them.

fact: {coworker2} starts gossiping about why another coworker was called into a meeting.
issues.action: Change the subject or say you would rather not guess about it.
issues.reason: Gossip spreads rumors and damages trust. Politely stepping away keeps you professional.

shortcut.text: Join in, since everyone is curious.
shortcut.why: Speculating about a coworker spreads rumors that can hurt them.
shortcut.mis: Gossip is harmless if everyone does it.

fact: A team meeting starts in two minutes, and you are about to start a long personal call.
issues.action: Save the call for your break and go to the meeting on time.
issues.reason: Arriving late to meetings wastes others' time and looks unreliable.
issues.lesson: Be on time for meetings; personal business can wait for breaks.

shortcut.text: Make the call and slip into the meeting late.
shortcut.why: Arriving late interrupts the meeting and shows little respect for the team.
shortcut.mis: Being a few minutes late does not matter.

fact: The uniform policy says to wear your name badge, and you left yours in your car.
issues.action: Get your name badge from the car before your shift starts.
issues.reason: The badge is part of the uniform policy and helps people know who you are.
issues.lesson: Follow uniform and badge policies every shift.

shortcut.text: Work without it, since everyone knows who you are.
shortcut.why: The policy applies every shift, and {client.plural} do not know you.
shortcut.mis: Policies only matter for new people.

proceed.text: Go ahead, since nobody else will be bothered.
proceed.why: In each case, other people are affected, so going ahead without thinking is not professional.
proceed.lesson: Professional etiquette means considering how your actions affect others.

generic.text: Ask {coworker3} whether it is okay and do whatever they say.
generic.why: A coworker's opinion does not replace your own judgment about etiquette.
generic.mis: If a coworker approves, it must be fine.

generic.text: Complain to {lead|the} about how stressful the day has been.
generic.why: Venting to the lead does not address the situation in front of you.

title: Your email to a new {client}
intro: You are about to email a new {client} for the first time. Check the message first.
doc.lesson: Professional emails are courteous, clear and represent the workplace well.

bad.why: A first message to a {client} should open respectfully.

lines.text: My name is {coworker}, and I will be your contact at {workplace|the}.

bad.text: Anyway, here is the stuff you need.
bad.why: Skipping any introduction leaves the new {client} unsure who is writing.

lines.text: Our meeting is confirmed for Tuesday at 10 a.m.

bad.text: hey, see u tues at like 10 or whatever
bad.why: Slang and missing capitalization are too casual for a first message to a {client}.

lines.text: Please bring any photos of the work you would like done.

bad.text: Bring photos, or do not bother coming.
bad.why: The line is rude and could drive the {client} away.
Overly familiar language is not appropriate for a first message to a {client}.

lines.text: Feel free to call if anything changes.

bad.text: Honestly, things here have been chaotic lately, so bear with us.
bad.why: Complaining about your workplace to a new {client} represents it poorly.

review.notes: Etiquette situations are beginner-only single decisions.
